claims.claim: The Age of Revolutions was a connected wave of Atlantic political revolutions in the later 18th and early 19th centuries that drew on shared Enlightenment ideas — natural rights, popular sovereignty, equality before the law, and opposition to inherited noble privilege, established-church dominance, and arbitrary royal authority.

The American Revolution (armed conflict 1775-1783) opened the era: colonists protested taxation without representation, the Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence in 1776, Britain surrendered at Yorktown in 1781, and independence was formalized by the Treaty of Paris in 1783.

In the French Revolution, Louis XVI summoned the Estates-General in 1789, the National Assembly issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen on August 26, 1789, the monarchy was abolished and the Republic proclaimed on September 21, 1792, Louis XVI was executed on January 21, 1793, the Reign of Terror ran from September 1793 to July 1794 under Robespierre's Committee of Public Safety, and Napoleon Bonaparte seized power in the coup of 18 Brumaire on November 9, 1799.

The Reign of Terror was the violent phase of the French Revolution: the Committee of Public Safety executed thousands (roughly 16,000-17,000 by guillotine, with far more imprisoned) before Robespierre himself was overthrown and executed on July 28, 1794.

The Haitian Revolution began with a mass uprising of enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue in August 1791; Toussaint Louverture emerged as its leader, revolutionary France abolished slavery in 1794, Napoleon sent an expedition in 1802 to restore French control and slavery, and after Toussaint's capture Jean-Jacques Dessalines declared independence on January 1, 1804, creating Haiti.

Haiti was the first independent nation to emerge from a large-scale slave revolt — the only such revolt in history to succeed in founding a state — and became the first independent Black republic and the second independent nation in the Americas after the United States.

The Latin American wars of independence were triggered when Napoleon's invasion of Spain during the Peninsular War (1808-1814) detained the Spanish king and provoked a crisis of legitimacy; local juntas formed across Spanish America and creole (American-born European-descended) elites led movements that, roughly between 1808 and 1826, won independence for most of Spanish America.

Simon Bolivar (1783-1830), called the Liberator, led the northern campaigns that freed Venezuela, New Granada (Colombia and Panama), Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia (named after him in 1825), while Jose de San Martin led the southern campaigns in Argentina, Chile, and Peru; the Battle of Ayacucho on December 9, 1824 effectively sealed Spanish South American independence.

The revolutions were marked by a defining contradiction between proclaimed universal rights and continued exclusion: American independence coexisted with slavery and the Three-Fifths Clause, revolutionary France granted rights only to certain men and reestablished colonial slavery under Napoleon, and Latin American creole leaders often limited their aims to White men of Spanish descent — while Haiti alone abolished slavery outright and extended citizenship across racial lines.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The exact span of the 'Age of Revolutions'
positions: Some frame it as the Atlantic revolutions c. 1775-1825 (American, French, Haitian, Spanish American)
Others extend the label to 1848 to include later European liberal and national revolutions
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as roughly 1775-1848 as an era label, with the lesson concentrating on the core Atlantic cluster (c. 1775-1825) named in scope, and noting the wider span rather than treating the dates as a fixed program.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The year France abolished colonial slavery
positions: The National Convention decreed abolition on February 4, 1794 (OpenStax and standard accounts)
Some popular summaries give 1795, reflecting when Toussaint Louverture aligned with republican France
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Used 1794 (the National Convention's decree), the well-established date, and did not repeat the 1795 figure that a secondary source attached to Toussaint's alignment rather than to the abolition decree.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft in lessons.json contained only generic boilerplate framing revolutions as 'a foundational concept in History' with no verifiable historical claims; all of its wording was discarded.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced placeholder 'concept' framing with a substantive, dated comparative account of four revolutions.
Gave the Haitian Revolution its due weight as the only successful large-scale slave revolt and the first independent Black republic, rather than treating it as a footnote to the French Revolution.

Foregrounded the liberty/slavery and inclusion/exclusion contradictions with concrete evidence (Three-Fifths Clause, Napoleon's restoration of colonial slavery, creole-limited aims), stated factually and without celebrating or sensationalizing revolutionary violence.
